newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan gets 14-1 vote for top U.N. post, France blocks.
newsitem.headline: Annan gets 14-1 vote for top U.N. post, France blocks.

text.p: Kofi Annan, the Ghanaian head of U.N. peacekeeping, on Thursday tightened his grip on the race for U.N. secretary-general but still was unable to shake off a potential French veto.

Diplomats said Annan's score on the second informal poll of the day was 14-1, with France presumed as the only holdout. This means he did as well as his boss, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who received the same vote when the U.S. vetoed him in an official poll on Nov. 19.

The 15-member Security Council held two rounds of unofficial polls on Thursday meant to "discourage" or "encourage" four declared candidates from Africa, which is given preference in fielding nominees. Boutros-Ghali has stepped aside temporarily from the polling.

To win, a candidate must have a minimum of nine votes and no veto from the council's five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France. In polls on Wednesday and Thursday, Annan was the only candidate to receive more than nine votes.
Another unofficial ballot will be taken on Friday. Boutros-Ghali's five-year term expires on Dec. 31.

Annan's closest rival was Amara Essy, the foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and the 1994-95 U.N. General Assembly president. He received 7 votes on Thursday, with two permanent members opposing him, presumably the United States and Britain.

The other two candidates, Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah, a former foreign minister of Mauritania, who was once the U.N. envoy to Burundi, and Hamid Algabid, a former Niger prime minister and the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, received 4 and 3 votes, respectively.

Said Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy: "The smoke coming out of the Security Council chimney this morning is once again black," a reference to the colour of the smoke after an inconclusive vote to elect a new pope.
"Up until this moment there are no new candidatures. Members of the council shall meet again to conduct more straw polls tomorrow," he said.
A U.S. official said after the poll: "We are even more encouraged that the encouraging-discouraging process works."
British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston said: "That was a very encouraging discussion." He said developments were moving in a positive direction.
And France's ambassador Alain Dejammet said only that the next secreatry-general would be an African. "We hope he will come from Africa and very likely, he will speak French."
All four candidates speak French but Annan is the only one from a English-speaking country.
French envoys privately say they have no particular grievance against Annan, who does speak French, but prefer other African candidates, such as Essy and Ould-Abdallah.

The next step, diplomats say, is to either convince France to change its mind or find a compromise candidate. President Jacques Chirac has already indicated he would veto Salim A. Salim, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity, because he does not speak French.

But envoys say France would be amenable to Lakhdar Brahimi, an Algerian, who last year ran the U.N. operation in Haiti, or Alassane Ouattara of the Ivory Coast, who is a vice president of the International Monetary Fund.

Another potential candidate is Olara Otunnu, the popular Ugandan-born head of the International Peace Academy, a New York-based think tank. Otunnu, now an Ivory Coast citizen, apparently faces opposition from Uganda.

The English-French feud at the United Nations escalated when Washington vetoed Boutros-Ghali, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister, author and French-educated law professor. U.S. officials maintain he is too weak in reforming the world body, a position shared by few other countries, and particularly not by France, his chief backer when he won election five years ago.
In turn, the United States and Britain this week voted against or abstained on the poll for the three other African candidates on the list, diplomats said.
Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4 and could reactivate it any time. But he is believed certain to be vetoed again by the United States.
